newsitem.title: FINLAND: MERITA SEES NO UPSETS FROM FAST GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: MERITA SEES NO UPSETS FROM FAST GROWTH.

text.p: Economists at Finland's biggest banking group Merita said on Tuesday the Finnish economy was free of domestic disturbance factors despite upping their 1997 GDP forecast to four percent from an earlier 3.5 percent.

"Although the pace of growth is picking up this much, we do not see any disequilibrium factors in Finland," Merita chief economist Juha Ahtola told a news conference on the publication of the bank's four-monthly economic forecast.
"Strength and stability are words that describe the Finnish economy now and in the period to come," Ahtola said.
The bank said in its forecast the Finnish economy appeared to have entered a phase of vigorous growth, with firm evidence of a pick-up in exports since late 1996.
"Exports have performed slightly better than expected (in 1996) but construction in particularly has taken off," Ahtola said.
The bank raised its forecast for 1997 export growth to seven percent from an earlier five percent and increased its forecast for investment to nine percent from eight percent.
The bank also upped its forecast for 1997 industrial production to six percent from four percent.
Merita sees economic growth rising to about five percent by mid-1997, and then settling back to about 3.5 percent in the second half, Ahtola said.
Predicting that construction would account for about 4.5 percent of GDP this year, up from less than 3.5 percent last year, Ahtola said the economy was "not sailing in dangerous waters" in this area.
With no domestic inflationary pressures in view, the bank said it also expected no big changes in monetary policy.
"In this economic situation, we do not see any indigenous reasons for easing monetary policy," said economist Sirpa Wallius.
Merita also slightly lowered its forecast for unemployment in 1997 to 15.2 percent from an earlier 15.5 percent, and predicted an unemployment rate of 14.3 percent in 1998.
